name: Diacetyl boldine

lead: Diacetyl boldine is an ingredient made from boldine, an alkaloid from the boldo tree. It appears in brightening serums aimed at dark spots and melasma.
Published human studies are few and test it inside multi-ingredient products, some compared against hydroquinone. Whether it works on its own has not been tested separately.

paras: A melasma study describes it as stabilizing tyrosinase, the enzyme that produces melanin, in its inactive form.

The sources reviewed report no specific adverse-event data for the ingredient. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, and trial registrations for serums that may contain it list no posted results.

Combined use of two formulations containing diacetyl boldine, TGF-β1 biomimetic oligopeptide-68 with other hypopigmenting/exfoliating agents and sunscreen provides effective and convenient treatment for facial melasma. Either is equal to or is better than 4% hydroquinone on normal skin.

lead: Diacetyl boldine (DAB) is a cosmetic skin-brightening ingredient derived from boldine, an aporphine alkaloid found in the bark of the boldo tree (Peumus boldus) [1]. It is used in serums and creams aimed at hyperpigmentation, dark spots and melasma, usually as one component of a multi-ingredient formula.

According to a published melasma study, DAB acts by stabilizing tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, in its inactive form [2]. Published human evidence is limited to a small number of formulation studies in which DAB was combined with other agents, so its effect on its own has not been isolated [3][2].
infobox: Keeps tyrosinase in an inactive form [2]
Topical serums and creams for hyperpigmentation

paras: Boldine is described as the most abundant alkaloid in boldo bark and is also found in Lindera aggregata [1]. Diacetyl boldine is its diacetylated derivative, developed for topical use. In the research literature it appears in brightening and anti-aging formulations alongside peptides, exfoliating agents and sunscreens [3][2].

A 2016 melasma study states that DAB stabilizes tyrosinase in its inactive form, while a companion ingredient, TGF-beta1 biomimetic oligopeptide-68, inhibits tyrosinase activity [2]. Tyrosinase is the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin synthesis.

A 2016 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined two formulations containing DAB and TGF-beta1 oligopeptide-68, used together with other hypopigmenting or exfoliating agents and sunscreen, on facial melasma. The same study compared them with 2% and 4% hydroquinone creams on sun-protected normal skin. The title reports that the formulations were equal to or better than 4% hydroquinone on normal skin [2].

A 2020 paper described a multifunctional skin care formulation combining anti-pollution, brightening and anti-aging active complexes [3]. Because several actives were combined in both studies, neither isolates DAB's own contribution.

Two registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov are listed as completed: a 4-week study of two brightening serums versus 4% hydroquinone in 18 women with hyperpigmentation (started 2025) [4], and a 16-week study of a dark spot corrector serum in 48 women (started 2024) [5]. The registrations do not themselves report results, and the listings do not state that DAB is the active ingredient.

A 2023 laboratory study developed a microemulsion for topical delivery of DAB, tested its permeation through excised human skin and measured cytotoxicity against a mouse melanoma cell line (B16BL6) in vitro, framing it as a possible chemoprotective approach [6]. This is cell and ex vivo work, not a human trial.
